The agency issued the registrations to more than 900 state-licensed dispensaries in Alabama,

Ancient Egyptians left clues for how they made "mummies" written in hieroglyphics.
Archaeologists are using chemistry to help decipher the code, NPR's Ping Wang reports.
The ancient Egyptians mummified their dead, preserving their bodies for thousands of years.
Much of the process remains a mystery, so researchers at Marburg University in Germany
decided to test samples from mummified heads and body parts found in museum
and historical collections. Ricardo Guirica, an Egyptologist,
says that chemical analysis turned up substances new to their understanding of mummification,
like extracts from aloe, which may shed light on at least one hieroglyphic symbol.
Maybe we can translate an "imi" which was not very sure beforehand now as aloe.
Aloes surprised them because it wasn't native to ancient Egypt.
It likely came from trade with regions near Ethiopia or Arabia.
The findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Ping Wang, NPR News.
